properties.decision:
Recorded as BRAINSTORMING, not as a proposal. Anthony, 2026-09-06, relaying an external analysis he found while searching 'graph db', which argued: (1) at 3,500 nodes / 20,000 edges performance is a wash — everything fits in RAM, any store is fast, so a graph database is not chosen for speed; (2) the real benefit is code elegance — a shortest-path or all-paths query is one line of Cypher versus nested recursive SQL; (3) schema flexibility — polymorphic entities without NULL-heavy tables; and (4) if Postgres is already in the stack, WITH RECURSIVE or the Apache AGE extension gives graph queries without a second database. Distinct from the Redis question (dec:idea-is-redis-a-third-backend-option...), which asked about a network KEY-VALUE store behind the same seam; this asks whether the store should be a graph DATABASE at all.

THE FOUR CLAIMS, CHECKED AGAINST WHAT REFLOW2 HAS MEASURED:
(1) 'Performance is a wash' — HALF TRUE HERE, and the half matters. TRUE: the byte store is not reflow2's bottleneck — fact:hydrate-cost-is-superlinear-in-edges-and-the-byte-store-is-not-the-bottleneck (95% of hydrate is import_graph, not the store) and fact:loop-status-after-a-write-is-distributed-intrinsic-analysis-with-no-single-lever (the ~7 s rollup is six detectors doing thousands of in-process point reads; the store answers each in ~100 ns). FALSE for a NETWORK database: those thousands of reads become thousands of round trips (the Redis idea costs this at +5-10 s per rollup). The article's 'anything is fast' assumes SET-ORIENTED queries pushed to the server in one round trip — which is exactly what a graph database's query language gives and a KV does not. So for an in-process store the claim holds and is moot; for a network store the query language is not ergonomics, it is the only thing that makes the network affordable.
(2) 'Code elegance' — TRUE OF THE MECHANICS, BESIDE THE POINT FOR THE PRODUCT. reflow2 already computes over an in-RAM graph it builds per sweep (graphalg: design_network, operational_network, Leiden communities, articulation points, cycles); shortest-path is a library call, not a hand-written CTE. The detectors ARE the product — their semantics (what an unallocated capability means, when a withdrawn node stops raising gaps, what a shared cause is) are the vocabulary's third leg. Moving them into Cypher strings moves the semantics out of typed Rust into query text, and the record of WHY each detector fires (the doc comments and facts they cite) with them.
(3) 'Schema flexibility' — A NON-BENEFIT AND A HAZARD HERE. cap:store is a schema-validated graph store on purpose; schema-first is rule 1 of the project; defaults-do-not-assert and the typed vocabulary are the design's spine. The freedom to attach any property to any node is the freedom the validator exists to refuse.
(4) 'Postgres + AGE' — SAME COST CLASS AS REDIS (an external daemon in a one-liner install story; a socket surface; Alex's TUI environment) with better pushdown; AGE is an extension to install on top. SQLite deserves the mention the article did not give: embedded, no daemon, bundled by rusqlite (C but compiles in seconds), recursive CTEs available, ordered keys — it meets the six-function KvBackend seam as well as RocksDB and answers dec:idea-a-byte-backend-that-compiles-in-seconds without a network.

THE OPTIONS, as they now stand across both brainstorms: (a) RocksDB (status quo, C++ build); (b) in-memory + export as truth (+ optional embedded store for startup); (c) an embedded store that compiles in seconds behind the SAME seam — redb, sled, SQLite; (d) a network KV — Redis; (e) a network graph database — Neo4j, or Postgres with CTEs / AGE — with traversals pushed to the server.
properties.name: OPEN — would a graph database (Neo4j; Postgres with recursive CTEs or Apache AGE) serve reflow2 better than a KV store behind KvBackend at ~3,500 nodes / ~20,000 edges — and which of the usual arguments for one actually hold here?
properties.rationale: A RANKING, AS A FINDING NOT A DECISION. The article's own headline — 'at this scale you will not be choosing for performance' — is an argument FOR the direction reflow2's earlier brainstorms already took: the graph fits in RAM, reflow2 already traverses it in RAM, so the STORE question is about DURABILITY and SHARING, not query power. That splits the options cleanly. If sharing across processes and machines is NOT required (the shared server suffices): (b) or (c) — nothing networked earns its daemon, and (e) additionally pulls the detectors' semantics into query strings and relaxes the schema the design depends on. If sharing IS required: (e) beats (d), because pushdown makes the network affordable where a KV's per-read round trips do not — but the price is either rewriting the detectors as Cypher/SQL or keeping them in Rust and still paying the round trips. NOT IN THE ARTICLE, and the real reflow2-specific point: the pain that keeps recurring here is not query power or speed, it is that THE DESIGN GRAPH DOES NOT BRANCH WITH GIT (one store per project directory shared by every branch; it bit this session four times) and that a fix can land without closing its finding. Neither a graph database nor a KV addresses those; they are data-model and process questions. NOT MEASURED: no graph-database or Postgres numbers here — the latency and pushdown claims are typical figures reasoned against reflow2's measured access pattern, not measured on it. Anthony rules; nothing is built.
